title: How to Choose a Dentist

imageAlt: A couple sitting across a desk from a professional, talking things through
body:
Choosing a dental practice is harder than it should be. Every website says similar things, review scores cluster together, and most people only find out what a practice is really like after they have committed to treatment.

Here is a more practical way to assess one, whether you are new to New Farm and the surrounding suburbs or simply looking for a change.

Start With the Practical Filters

These are the easy ones, and they matter more than people expect, because a practice you cannot get to at a time that suits you is a practice you will stop attending.

  • Location and parking. Is it realistic on a workday? Is parking free, paid or non-existent?
  • Opening hours. Do they offer times outside your working hours?
  • Range of care. Can they handle general, cosmetic, restorative and emergency work, or will you be referred out frequently?
  • Emergency availability. Do they keep time for urgent problems? Our Emergency Dentistry page explains how we approach this.
  • Who they see. If you have children, does the practice provide children's dentistry?
  • Health funds. Do they accept your fund, process claims on the spot, and are they a preferred provider?

Look at Who Will Treat You

All dentists in Australia are registered with the Dental Board of Australia, and you can check any practitioner's registration on the Ahpra public register. It takes a minute and confirms their qualifications and whether there are any conditions on their registration.

Beyond registration, look at continuing education and areas of interest. Dentistry changes, and practitioners who regularly undertake further training tend to be the ones offering current approaches rather than the ones they learned twenty years ago.

Questions Worth Asking Before You Commit

You can ask these on the phone before booking:

  • How long is a new patient appointment, and what does it include?
  • Do you provide written treatment plans with costs before treatment begins?
  • Will I see the same dentist each visit?
  • How do you handle emergencies for existing patients?
  • What is your approach with nervous patients?
  • Do you offer payment plans or accept my health fund?

The answers matter less than how they are answered. A practice that explains things clearly on the phone usually explains things clearly in the chair.

What a Good First Appointment Feels Like

By the end of a first visit, you should:

  • Have been asked about your medical history and your concerns before anything was examined
  • Have had a thorough examination, including a check of your gums and soft tissues, not just a quick look for cavities
  • Understand what was found, ideally having been shown images or X-rays
  • Know what, if anything, is recommended, why, and what the alternatives are
  • Have a written plan with costs, if treatment is needed
  • Not feel pressured to decide on the spot

If you leave unsure what was found or why something is recommended, that is useful information in itself.

Warning Signs

  • A large treatment plan presented at a first visit with urgency attached
  • Costs that are vague, or quoted only for part of the treatment
  • Reluctance to show you what they are seeing, or to explain alternatives
  • Any suggestion that seeking a second opinion would be unreasonable
  • Recommendations to replace sound restorations for health reasons without clear evidence
  • Marketing built on superlatives rather than information

A second opinion is a normal part of healthcare. No reputable practitioner is offended by one.

On Reviews

Reviews can tell you something about communication, waiting times and front-desk experience. They tell you very little about clinical quality, because patients are not in a position to assess that, and the results of dental treatment often become apparent years later.

Treat them as one data point among several rather than the deciding factor. Under Australian advertising rules for health services, practices cannot use patient testimonials in their own advertising, which is why you will not see them on our site.

What Matters Most Over Time

The practices people stay with for decades tend to share a few things: they explain rather than instruct, they are conservative with healthy teeth, they are transparent about cost, they keep good records so changes can be tracked, and they are reachable when something goes wrong.

Moving Practices

If you decide to change, the transition is simpler than people assume.

You are entitled to your dental records, including X-rays. Ask your previous practice to send them to your new one, or request copies yourself. There is no need to explain why you are leaving, and no practice should make it awkward.

Bringing recent X-rays avoids repeating imaging unnecessarily and gives your new dentist a history to compare against. If you have had significant treatment, a short written summary of what was done and when is useful too.

Do not wait until something hurts to make the change. A routine first visit gives you and the practice a baseline, which is far better than meeting for the first time during an emergency.

Come and See Us

If you are looking for a practice near New Farm, you can read more About Precision Dental, or just book a check-up and clean and judge for yourself. Our Prices and Payment Options page sets out fees and payment methods, and our Dentist New Farm page covers visiting us from the area. Call Precision Dental on {{site:phone}} or book online.

faq.q: How do I check a dentist's registration?
a: Search their name on the Ahpra public register. It confirms they are registered with the Dental Board of Australia and shows any conditions on their registration.

faq.q: What should happen at a first dental appointment?
a: Your medical history and concerns should be discussed, a thorough examination carried out, findings explained, and a written plan with costs provided if treatment is needed.

faq.q: Are online reviews a good guide to a dentist?
a: They can tell you about communication and service, but very little about clinical quality. Treat them as one piece of information among several.

faq.q: Is it okay to get a second opinion?
a: Yes. A second opinion is a normal part of healthcare, and no reputable practitioner should be offended by one.

faq.q: How do I transfer my dental records?
a: Ask your previous practice to send your records and X-rays to your new practice, or request copies yourself. You do not need to give a reason.

faq.q: What are warning signs when choosing a dentist?
a: Large treatment plans presented with urgency at a first visit, vague or partial costs, reluctance to explain alternatives, and pressure to decide on the spot.
